principles.text: Choppy, selective market: strong names gapping higher while weak names bounce into the declining 9; 'maybe some shorts can work well and some longs can work well, but no trend in most names.' Still leaning short but more open-minded.
Not a fan of buying at a declining weekly 60/150 EMA (crypto); wait for the pullback into the faster EMAs (13/20/30 on that chart) instead.

Joke, not a rule: a viewer said 'be glad you didn't have buying power to short Tesla' and he laughed that the trades he can't afford tend to be the ones that don't work. He would have taken the TSLA short if he had buying power; it happening to fail is coincidence.
Stop asking 'what do you think about X' - build your own opinion and let the market judge it; the reasoning process matters more than the conclusion, especially from 'a guy with a 25% win rate.'

SNDK short logic: group weakness (SK Hynix under all supports), weekly emphasis, and the dot-com analog - leaders form a bullish-looking pattern (cup/VCP/inside-week breakout) after the first leg down, and top after that breakout fails or the range breaks down. Markets move faster now, so worth a few tries.
Rarely buys a pullback purely off the 50 EMA (tried it on cyber names, still not good at it); prefers a pullback into an EMA convergence where the 9/21/50 sit close together.

Routine: at the desk 30 minutes before the open with a quick checklist; scans, watchlist review and trade planning happen while the market is closed (Hong Kong morning, 30-60 min) to stay rational; journal right after the scans.
Stocks don't 'belong' to an index; the index helps time entries a little but isn't required. Most of his watchlist is tech and correlates with QQQ, and QQQ/SPY are highly correlated anyway.

Semis are somewhat extended to the downside but haven't shown a real volatility expansion (no -3% to -5% wide red candles); the current range contraction should be followed by an expansion, which is the trade on memory names, QQQ, SPY and IWM.

Cover most (not all) shorts when QQQ closes strong above the 9/21 EMA and the gap level (~715) - the key level for short-term strength; reduce short exposure to protect profits, without becoming bullish.

Opening range breakouts: pull the trigger when the 1-minute opening range is tight (under ~1.5% stop); when the first candle already spans 4-5% it's the hardest kind. Alternative entry: 1-minute pullback into the opening-range high.
Watchlist sizes today: 55 lagging / 31 mediocre / 46 leading. Counts grow in bull markets and shrink in corrections as names fall below the $200M dollar-volume threshold and move to tier 2.
Pullback buys that go sideways: it's part of the game (8-9 of 10 can fail to follow through). When that happens the market is choppy or you're in the wrong stocks (defensives like KO don't trend).
Silver/gold short: don't be early - want at least 15-minute (or 30-min/hourly) lows below the 9 EMA before shorting the rally into the anchored VWAP.

A tiny stop that shakes you out (viewer's NVDA short) is what saves you if the name runs to 300; if NVDA really rejects here there will be plenty of entries through the 9/21/50, and when the strongest name cracks, other names will too.

Re-entry after a stop-out: no systematic rule. Re-short if the name quickly reverses (5-minute long wick turning red) and the market/other shorts agree; don't re-short once it clears the swing high and the anchored VWAP (SPCX).
Uses no breadth metrics - they add noise to decision making.
Pre-calculate position size for a 1% stop and a 1.5% stop (e.g. 5k vs 3k) and interpolate for anything in between (1.3% stop -> ~4k).

Returns can't be compared across traders or years: higher return = higher drawdown, and each year favors a different style. Only advice: keep fixing your mistakes, minimize downside, and let the market give the reward.
He wants a choppy, difficult market: those are the periods that expose weaknesses and force improvement.
